rationale: Schizophrenia EEG shows narrow-band changes: a slower, weaker alpha peak, more delta/theta, and shifts between beta sub-bands. The five broad bands blur these together, so I'm replacing them with 2-Hz-wide log relative-power bins from 1 to 45 Hz. Because this adds many correlated features, the logistic-regression C is now picked by inner grouped CV on the training fold, which the brief allows.

These ASEEG recordings had no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or muscle bursts can dominate the mean-averaged Welch spectrum. That mostly inflates delta and gamma power, which hides the subtle delta/theta increase and alpha reduction seen in schizophrenia. I'm switching Welch to median averaging across the 2-s segments, which gives a robust spectrum per subject. This should also help on the external sets, which come from different clinics with different artifact levels and recording lengths.

Schizophrenia is often described as a disorder of disconnection. Resting EEG in patients shows changed phase coupling in the theta and alpha bands, and the current spectral model cannot see this. I'm adding per-channel node strength of the weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) in the delta, theta, alpha and beta bands. The EEG is first re-referenced to the common average, and the wPLI is computed from 2-s epochs. wPLI ignores amplitude scale and zero-lag volume conduction, which should help on the external amplifiers and references. Averaging over each channel's links keeps the number of new features at 64 rather than 480 pairwise values, which suits a training set of about 80 subjects.

Many studies report that EEG complexity is altered in schizophrenia. Spectral power and wPLI do not capture this nonlinear signal irregularity, so I'm adding one Higuchi fractal dimension per channel. It is computed on the common-average-referenced EEG after a 1–45 Hz band-pass, over 10-s epochs, and I take the median across epochs. Fractal dimension does not depend on amplitude scale, and the median makes it robust to artifacts and to recording length, which matters for the external sets. It adds only 16 features, which suits a training set of about 80 subjects.

Resting-state EEG microstate changes are among the best-replicated EEG markers of schizophrenia: class D is shorter and less frequent, and class C is more prominent. The current spectral and wPLI features cannot see these brief whole-scalp topographic dynamics. I'm adding microstate features computed on the eyes-closed EEG after average referencing and a 2–20 Hz filter. Four group template maps are fitted label-free on unit-normalized maps taken at GFP peaks, using polarity-invariant modified k-means. The templates are matched to canonical A–D topographies built from 10-20 electrode positions, so their order stays stable across datasets. Each subject then gets coverage, mean duration and occurrence rate per class, plus total GEV, which adds 13 features. These features do not depend on amplitude scale, and rates and fractions do not depend on recording length, which should help on the external sets.

Two well-replicated schizophrenia EEG markers are not represented by the current features: a slower individual alpha peak frequency and a flatter aperiodic (1/f) exponent, which is thought to reflect a change in the balance of excitation and inhibition. I'm adding a FOOOF-like spectral parameterization of the eyes-closed EEG after average referencing. For each channel it fits a robust log-log line from 2 to 40 Hz with the alpha range excluded, which gives the exponent, and then takes the centre of gravity of the above-fit residual from 7 to 13 Hz, which gives the alpha peak frequency. That adds 32 features, and neither depends on amplitude scale or recording length.

The 189 features currently go into one logistic regression, so the 80 band-power and 64 wPLI features take most of the shrinkage budget. The 13 microstate and 32 aperiodic/alpha-peak features, which are well-replicated schizophrenia markers, get comparatively little weight. I'm replacing it with late fusion: a separate standardized L2 logistic regression for each feature family (band power, wPLI, spectral parameterization, microstates), with their log-odds averaged. Each physiological family then gets an equal vote. Small-n models with fewer features per model should also overfit less and carry over better to the external sites.

The model has no Riemannian covariance feature yet. I'm adding the tangent-space vector of one 4–13 Hz (theta+alpha) spatial covariance matrix per subject, computed on eyes-closed data after average referencing. It captures whole-montage linear coupling and spatial structure that per-channel node strengths and microstates miss, and schizophrenia shows altered theta/alpha connectivity. To keep it robust externally, each matrix is trace-normalized so amplitude scale drops out, the highest-variance epochs are dropped as likely artifacts, and the matrix is shrunk so it is always full rank. The reference point is the label-free log-Euclidean mean of all items' matrices, the same way the microstate templates are built.

The single 4–13 Hz Riemannian tangent-space covariance gave the biggest gain so far, but it can't see the increased beta-band power and coupling seen in schizophrenia, which is partly driven by antipsychotic medication and so should also show up in the external clinical cohorts. I'm adding a second tangent-space vector from a 13–30 Hz covariance, built the same way: eyes-closed data, average reference, trace-normalized, shrunk, high-variance epochs dropped, with a label-free log-Euclidean mean as the reference point per band.

I'm adding the 12 microstate transition probabilities P(next class j | current class i) to the 13 microstate features we already have. They are computed from the eyes-closed segment sequence using the existing label-free canonical A–D templates. Altered microstate syntax in schizophrenia, especially transitions into and out of classes C and D, is a replicated finding (Lehmann 2005, Nishida 2013). Coverage, duration and occurrence can't show it. The probabilities are fractions within each subject, so they don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which matters for the external sets.

I'm adding per-channel node strength of orthogonalized amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC; Hipp 2012) in the theta, alpha and beta bands, computed on eyes-closed data after average referencing. Schizophrenia is linked to altered amplitude coupling, which is a different mechanism from the phase-lag coupling that wPLI measures and the zero-lag linear coupling the covariance captures. Orthogonalizing removes volume conduction, using log power envelopes makes the feature independent of amplitude scale, and dropping the 10% highest-variance epochs gives some robustness to artifacts, recording length and amplifier at the external sites. This adds 48 features.

Every other feature family is already computed on the common average reference, but the relative band powers still use each recording's original reference, so their spatial pattern shifts with the reference montage. I'm average-referencing the EEG before the Welch band-power step. This should give the band powers a consistent, reference-free topography across subjects in the dev pool and at the external clinics (MSU, RepOD), which use different references. I haven't run it yet, so its effect on the Dev score (currently 0.902) is unknown.

The fixed C=0.1 was set back when the model had 80 band-power features, but the feature vector has since grown to about 345 dimensions, including 136 tangent-space features. With only about 80 training subjects, the right amount of L2 shrinkage has probably changed. I'm now picking C for the logistic regression by grouped 5-fold inner CV on the training fold only, using `groups_train` and pooled out-of-fold AUROC; ties go to the stronger penalty. This is a regularization change only; the feature pipeline is untouched. Round 1 also tuned C, but together with 2-Hz bins, so the two effects were never separated.

I'm adding a small set of graph-topology summaries computed on the eyes-closed wPLI matrices we already build. Weighted clustering, global efficiency and node-strength heterogeneity are computed for each of the 4 bands on mean-normalized weights, so they describe the network's shape independently of its overall coupling level. Lost small-world organization (lower clustering, longer paths) is a replicated finding in schizophrenia (Micheloyannis 2006, Rubinov 2009), and per-node strength cannot show it. This adds only 12 features, all scale-invariant, so it should not dilute the strong tangent-space signal the way the larger feature blocks did. I haven't run it, so its effect on the Dev score (currently 0.902) is unknown.

Relative alpha power mixes two things: a weaker alpha oscillation and a different aperiodic (1/f) background. The spectral parameterization already fits that background, but it only outputs the exponent and the peak frequency. I'm adding, for each channel, the alpha peak height above the aperiodic fit (the log10 maximum of the residual between 7 and 13 Hz). Reduced oscillatory alpha relative to background is a reported schizophrenia marker, and this measure does not depend on amplitude scale or reference gain. It adds only 16 features, so it should not dilute the model the way larger blocks did.

The 4–13 Hz Riemannian tangent-space feature gave the biggest gain so far, but its covariance is an arithmetic mean over epochs. That lets the highest-power epochs dominate it, such as alpha bursts, drowsiness or leftover artifacts. I'm changing it to a per-subject log-Euclidean (geometric) mean of per-epoch covariances, with each epoch trace-normalized and shrunk first. Every epoch then counts equally toward the spatial structure, outlying epochs are damped, and the estimate should be less sensitive to amplitude scale and recording length, which matters for the short external recordings. I haven't run this, so its effect on the Dev score (currently 0.902) is unknown.

I'm adding one detrended-fluctuation-analysis (DFA) exponent per channel, computed on the eyes-closed alpha (8–13 Hz) amplitude envelope after average referencing and fitted over 1–10 s windows. Schizophrenia is reported to weaken the long-range temporal correlations of alpha amplitude (Nikulin et al. 2012). No current feature captures this; band power, wPLI, covariance and microstates all describe static or sub-second structure. The exponent ignores amplitude scale, and the 1–10 s fit range still works on the 1-minute external recordings. It adds only 16 features.

Nikulin et al. (2012) found weaker long-range temporal correlations in schizophrenia in both the alpha and the beta amplitude envelopes. The alpha-envelope DFA was kept in round 17, so I'm adding the same per-channel DFA exponent for the beta (13–30 Hz) envelope: eyes closed, average reference, 1–10 s windows. It adds only 16 features and doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length.

I'm adding one permutation entropy per channel, computed on the eyes-closed EEG (average reference, 1–45 Hz band-pass, order 4, lag 2, top 10% variance epochs dropped). Schizophrenia is reported to change the ordinal-pattern complexity of resting EEG, which none of the current spectral, phase, covariance, microstate or DFA features capture. It adds only 16 features, and because it uses only the rank order of samples, it is unaffected by amplitude scale or amplifier gain and stable for short recordings, which matters for the external sets. The "entropy" family has not been tried yet, and I haven't run this, so its effect on the Dev score (currently 0.906) is unknown.

wPLI weights each epoch's cross-spectrum by its imaginary-part magnitude, so a few high-amplitude blink, movement or muscle epochs in these unprocessed recordings can take over the phase-lag estimate. I'm dropping the 10% highest-variance 2-s epochs before computing wPLI node strength, the same artifact rule the Riemannian covariance already uses. This should make the connectivity features reflect cortical coupling rather than artifacts, and make them steadier across the external clinics' different artifact levels. I haven't run it, so its effect on the Dev score is unknown.
